extracted.intended_audience: writers and readers interested in fiction craft books / creative-writing practitioners
extracted.subtask_description: A blog review assessing John Gardner's The Art of Fiction, extracting usable craft advice and critiquing the book's assumptions, examples, and exercises for contemporary writers. Focus is on what the book recommends for fiction-writing technique and where it falls short.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fiction as a 'vivid and continuous dream'
rubrics_metrics.description: Fiction should be a 'vivid and continuous dream' for readers; the writer's goal is to avoid disrupting the dream by any false note (unless that disruption is intentional).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Keep the reader enchanted; revision and editing aim to eliminate false notes that break immersion. Anti-pattern: lapses that pull the reader out of the fictional dream. Note that intentional disruption can be a valid technique if done deliberately (e.g., metafiction).

rubrics_metrics.name: Use repetition to enhance meaning and achieve a 'resonant close'
rubrics_metrics.description: The novel, like a symphony, can make good use of repetition to enhance meaning and, especially, to achieve a 'resonant close.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Read your work repeatedly 'watching for subtle meanings, connections, accidental repetitions, psychological significance' and then nudge these elements closer to the surface. Be tasteful about repetition; overuse or heavy-handed repetition is an anti-pattern.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid 'filter words' — give unmediated description
rubrics_metrics.description: Writers should be wary of 'filter words' that put the veil of the character's consciousness between the reader and the thing described.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer unmediated phrasings unless the act of noticing is important. Example contrast from the page: 'Turning, she noticed two snakes fighting in among the rocks.' vs 'She turned. In among the rocks, two snakes were fighting.' Use the latter for direct description; use filter words only when the character's perception/action matters to the scene.

rubrics_metrics.name: Control narrative/psychic distance
rubrics_metrics.description: Altering 'the distance the reader feels between himself and the events in the story' creates a range of effects; reducing distance can subsume the reader into the narratorial voice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Experiment with varying degrees of distance to achieve intended emotional or psychological effects (the page gives an example that gradually reduces distance until the narratorial 'you' takes over). Use distance deliberately: closer distance can increase immediacy and identification; greater distance can create irony or commentary.

rubrics_metrics.name: Diction: avoid inappropriate diction and diction shifts
rubrics_metrics.description: Diction problems (diction shifts and steady use of inappropriate diction) are presented as serious faults that suggest bad taste, inexperience, or timidity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose diction appropriate to voice, character, and genre; watch for inconsistent diction and shifts that jar the reader. Gardner frames such problems as symptomatic of defects in the writer's character or education — the functional guidance is to cultivate appropriate, consistent diction through reading and practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid 'faults of soul' (sentimentality, frigidity, mannerism)
rubrics_metrics.description: Gardner identifies 'faults of soul' — sentimentality, frigidity, and mannerism — as serious artistic failings. A 'frigid' writer 'lacks the kind of passion all true artists possess' and cannot enter deeply into characters' feelings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Strive for genuine emotional engagement and avoid mannered, artificial, or sentimental writing that prevents readers from connecting. Anti-patterns: emotionally flat (frigid) narration, overwrought sentimentality, or repetitive mannerisms that reveal artistic affectation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Precision of intention and execution ('knife-thrower' analogy)
rubrics_metrics.description: Perfection in craft is compared to a circus knife-thrower: 'Perfection means hitting exactly what you are aiming at and not touching by a hair what you are not.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be precise in what you intend to achieve with language, structure, and detail; avoid unintended effects. This calls for disciplined revision and careful control over technique so each element does exactly what you intend it to do.

rubrics_metrics.name: Genre/audience suitability — target 'serious literary artists'
rubrics_metrics.description: Gardner states the book is 'not for the writer of nurse books or thrillers or porno or the cheaper sort of sci-fi' but 'for serious literary artists.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be aware of intended audience and genre; techniques appropriate for literary art may differ from commercial-genre conventions. Warning: technical elegance applied through a 'junk mind' becomes 'elegant junk techniques' — craft must be matched with substantive purpose and taste.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use exercises to practice craft, but watch for taste and usefulness
rubrics_metrics.description: The book closes with suggested exercises ranging from very general ('18. Plot a novel') to extremely specific and potentially tasteless ('24. Without an instant’s lapse of taste, describe a person [a] going to the bathroom, [b] vomiting, [c] murdering a child').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exercises can hone skill, but evaluate exercises for constructive focus and appropriateness. Anti-patterns: exercises that are too vague to be actionable or that encourage gratuitous, tasteless material without pedagogical purpose.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid chauvinistic/unrepresentative language and portrayals
rubrics_metrics.description: The book repeatedly uses the 'universal he' and often fails to see women as creators; examples include stereotyped or problematic depictions of women (e.g., middle-aged housewife, 'well-preserved' stripper).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Modern writers should use inclusive language and portray subjects (including women) as creators and full characters rather than stereotypes. Be attentive to whose perspectives are centered and how examples may perpetuate bias or exclusion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Establish rapport with readers (craft books/self-help overlap)
rubrics_metrics.description: Craft books, like self-help books, must immediately establish rapport with readers — show them they are seen, understood, and welcomed with all of their flaws.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When writing craft guidance (or instructional material), address readers empathetically and make clear how the material applies to them; choose resources congenial to your needs because you're more likely to learn from books that feel welcoming.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tastefulness — avoid gratuitous tastelessness
rubrics_metrics.description: Gardner and the reviewer repeatedly emphasize 'taste' — admonitions like 'be tasteful' appear alongside examples and exercises.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exercise discretion in subject matter and imagery; avoid gratuitous shock or tastelessness unless it serves a clear artistic purpose. Anti-patterns: sensational or pornographic detail offered for its own sake rather than for narrative or thematic necessity.
